Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

let BadIPs     = dynamic(["142.93.242.144", "144.31.53.78", "198.13.159.44", "199.91.221.42"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["authorized-logins.net", "mail.authorized-logins.net", "php.authorized-logins.net", "sss.authorized-logins.net", "updater-worelos.com", "mails.updater-worelos.com", "defs.updater-worelos.com", "upd-domain-goloro.com", "mailes.upd-domain-goloro.com", "ftps.upd-domain-goloro.com"]);

   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer

status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

ENDPOINT

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:

author: Clankerusecase

    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows

    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:

            - '\svchost.exe'

let BadHashes = dynamic(["1e41c7bfaa6aa3b93b6cc024274a10e33f3e12fe7c98c1db387ef8927f9d1984", "34d798a6c55e57ed0932b6499f4fbcb5454bdfca903307be101a0594b0ac07bc", "3f797a639bc855bc6d5471f327924b62d10900ddec49b970eca6604142bbb4be", "59e3c4cb06331b4f2d78a9a0592f3747e573bd01c5a7650c26361d1e25520712", "8c935feec4bd05d5d918df308be417532fb42608fb989a08eab183e0ae699235", "afd5f1ed45a9867daf3bc64152cef460a06b164c8183e490db39146d4749a82c", "db972979d508e75fe730d3b72c2701470fbdaeaf8ebdd674744754fa44438ca5", "f591275a8f014b29e567529d67c54eb7bb4473db1c38737d6bfd5b3d52c9344e", "fb3630822b70bacb56aa4cec29b5a0e3e9acb3920809e70310a4003385a6d34a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"

           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),

                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mass npm Supply Chain Attack: 20 Leo Platform Packages Compromised

StepSecurity
2026-06-25 7 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

On June 24, 2026, an attacker published malicious versions of 20 npm packages belonging to the Leo Platform ecosystem in a coordinated burst spanning less than three seconds. All 20 packages carry an identical CI/CD attack toolkit that steals secrets from GitHub Actions runners, cloud credential stores, package registries, and password managers, then exfiltrates them via the victim's own GitHub token. Together these packages receive approximately 13,600 downloads per week.

Bun v1.3.13 runtime pulled from GitHub Releases during npm install (Phantom Gyp staging) AICommand & Control High
Hunts the Leo Platform / Miasma toolkit fetching the pinned Bun v1.3.13 single-file binary from github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases during a node/npm install. The stealer runs its core logic under this downloaded Bun runtime specifically to evade Node-child monitoring, so an install-context process reaching this exact release URL is a high-fidelity stager signal. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact version-pinned Bun download URL (github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1.3.13/) scoped to install-tooling initiators; Snyk and Microsoft both confirm the downloaded-Bun evasion for the same toolkit. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://snyk.io/blog/bun-based-stealer-hits-sap-cap-js-mbt-npm-packages/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/20/mini-shai-hulud-compromised-antv-npm-packages-enable-ci-cd-credential-theft/
ATT&CKT1105 T1195.002
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate projects that genuinely vendor Bun v1.3.13 and download it during CI build (e.g. Bun-based test suites)
  • Internal mirror/proxy caching the Bun release that then serves it to many build agents
  • Developer manually pinning bun-v1.3.13 in a setup script invoked by npm postinstall of a trusted package
  • Renovate/Dependabot dry-run installs that fetch toolchains
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun-types","@biomejs") and DeviceName startswith "trusted-bun-ci")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the package + version being installed when the download fired (correlate InitiatingProcessCommandLine / build log) and confirm whether the repo legitimately uses Bun; check the host against the 20 Leo Platform packages and the 2026-06-24T23:04:55Z publish window. 2) Contain: isolate/cordon the runner, revoke the GITHUB_TOKEN and any cloud creds (AWS/GCP/Azure/Vault) reachable from it, and rotate npm publish tokens for accounts that ran the build. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/account for bun executing /tmp/p*.js, /proc/<pid>/mem reads of Runner.Worker, and sudoers NOPASSWD writes; search the org for any leo-* package at the malicious versions in package-lock files.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1.3.13", "bun-v1.3.13")

| order by TimeGenerated desc

GitHub Actions Runner.Worker memory read via /proc/<pid>/mem (CI secret unmasking) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the toolkit locating the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker process and reading /proc/<pid>/mem directly (sometimes via a sudo python3 helper) to recover secrets that are masked in workflow logs. Reading another process's /proc memory on a CI runner is definitively malicious and is the campaign's core credential-access step. Rationale: Uses the article's definitive CI indicator (read of /proc/{pid}/mem where the target is Runner.Worker); the regex on /proc/<pid>/mem captures both the direct-read and sudo-python3 helper variants documented by Microsoft for the same toolkit. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/20/mini-shai-hulud-compromised-antv-npm-packages-enable-ci-cd-credential-theft/
ATT&CKT1003.007 T1212
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate debuggers/profilers (gdb, perf, gcore) attaching to a process during a build-time crash dump
  • Container/runtime health tooling snapshotting memory for diagnostics
  • Security agents themselves enumerating /proc (allowlist the EDR/AV process)
  • Coredump collection scripts that copy /proc/<pid>/mem ranges
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gdb","gcore","perf","mdatp","wdavdaemon","crash")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reader is NOT a known debugger/EDR and that the target PID resolves to Runner.Worker (check /proc/<pid>/cmdline access just before); treat any read in a GitHub Actions context as confirmed. 2) Contain: kill the runner, revoke the workflow GITHUB_TOKEN/OIDC token immediately and rotate every secret exposed to that workflow (cloud keys, registry tokens, 1Password items). 3) Hunt: look for the preceding Bun v1.3.13 download and subsequent GitHub GraphQL writes to newly-created dead-drop repos under the build's own token, and check for npm bypass_2fa republish activity.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/proc/[0-9]+/mem"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage matches regex @"/proc/[0-9]+/mem"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, ProcessName, ProcessID, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Passwordless sudo backdoor written for runner account (runner ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL) AIInstallation High
Hunts the toolkit granting itself passwordless sudo on GitHub-hosted runners by writing 'runner ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL' into the sudoers configuration. The exact account+NOPASSWD string is a narrow, high-fidelity privilege-escalation indicator unique to this campaign's runner targeting. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim escalation string 'runner ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL'; matching NOPASSWD:ALL plus the runner principal keeps it tight to this campaign's GitHub-hosted-runner targeting rather than generic sudoers edits. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mass-npm-supply-chain-attack-20-leo-platform-packages-compromised • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm
ATT&CKT1548.003 T1098
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Provisioning/IaC (Ansible, cloud-init) that legitimately grants the runner/build user NOPASSWD sudo on self-hosted runners
  • Container base-image build steps adding a NOPASSWD entry for a service account named runner
  • Admins troubleshooting sudo on a CI host
  • Vendor runner setup scripts that intentionally configure passwordless sudo
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ansible","cloud-init","python3-ansible","chef-client","puppet")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the sudoers write originated from a known provisioning tool/parent (Ansible, cloud-init) or from a build/npm-install descendant; the latter is malicious. 2) Contain: remove the sudoers entry, terminate the runner, and rotate credentials reachable from it; for ephemeral GitHub-hosted runners assume the runner is fully compromised and tear it down. 3) Hunt: correlate with the same host's Bun v1.3.13 download, /proc/<pid>/mem reads, and any GitHub Actions workflow files modified to add id-token: write and attacker-pinned action SHAs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine contains "NOPASSWD:ALL" and ProcessCommandLine has "runner"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine contains "NOPASSWD:ALL" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "runner"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Bun executes dropped temp payload /tmp/p*.js (Miasma stealer launch) AIExploitation High
Hunts the downloaded Bun runtime executing the toolkit's dropped payload at /tmp/p*.js — the definitive behavioral indicator that the obfuscated stealer logic has launched out-of-band from the Node install process. Bun running a script out of /tmp during a package install is anomalous and campaign-specific. Rationale: Uses the article's stated payload drop/exec location (/tmp/p*.js executed by bun) tied to the bun binary name; this parent-runtime + temp-path JS combination is the campaign's definitive behavioral execution indicator and near-zero in normal builds. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mass-npm-supply-chain-attack-20-leo-platform-packages-compromised • https://snyk.io/blog/bun-based-stealer-hits-sap-cap-js-mbt-npm-packages/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running an ad-hoc Bun script saved under /tmp during local debugging
  • CI scratch scripts written to /tmp and executed by a Bun-based build that happen to match the p*.js pattern
  • Test harnesses that generate temp .js fixtures and run them under Bun
  • Bun's own cache/transpile artifacts if relocated to /tmp
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","npm","node-gyp","sh","bash","yarn","pnpm")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the /tmp/p*.js contents (or its hash) before it self-deletes and confirm the parent chain is node/npm install rather than an intentional Bun project. 2) Contain: kill the bun process and runner, revoke the workflow token and rotate all cloud/registry/Vault/1Password secrets exposed to the job. 3) Hunt: pivot to the host's outbound Bun v1.3.13 download, /proc/<pid>/mem Runner.Worker reads, sudoers NOPASSWD writes, and any npm publishes via bypass_2fa from accounts that ran the build; scan repos for leo-* packages pinned to the malicious versions.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "bun"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/tmp/p[^/ ]*\.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has "bun"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/tmp/p[^/ ]*\.js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)

        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,

// Article-specific bespoke detection — Mass npm Supply Chain Attack: 20 Leo Platform Packages Compromised
// Hunts the actual binaries / paths / commandline fragments named
// in the article instead of a generic technique-class template.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("index.js"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,
          FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

// File-creation events for the named binaries / paths
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FolderPath has_any ("/dev/null") or FileName in~ ("index.js"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath,
          FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Gamaredon HTA downloader auto-executing from Startup folder at logon (mshta.exe) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Gamaredon WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 ADS path-traversal dropping HTA/VBS into Startup folder · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Gamaredon dead-drop C&C resolution via Telegra.ph and GoFile from script hosts · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Gamaredon stealer exfiltration to S3-compatible cloud storage (Wasabi/Tebi/Intercolo) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Gamaredon WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 ADS path-traversal dropping HTA/VBS into Startup folder AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence step Gamaredon adopted from 2025-09-26: a malicious RAR archive exploiting WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 (alternate-data-stream path traversal) to write an HTA/VBS/VBE/LNK downloader into the user's Startup folder so it auto-runs at next login. Article-specific because it pins the writing process to WinRAR-family binaries and the target to the Startup directory. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete persistence pivot (CVE-2025-8088 → HTA/VBS into Startup folder, active from 2025-09-26) and the WinRAR extraction binaries; Mandiant/Google and SOC Prime confirm the same ADS-to-Startup write pattern (.hta/.vbs/.vbe) across multiple Russia-aligned actors, so it is second-sourced. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/exploiting-critical-winrar-vulnerability • https://socprime.com/active-threats/cve-2025-8088-critical-winrar-vulnerability/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/winrar-path-traversal-flaw-still-exploited-by-numerous-hackers/amp/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1203 T1564.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate installers shipped as RAR self-extractors that legitimately add a startup launcher
  • IT-deployed login scripts (.vbs/.lnk) packaged in archives by an admin
  • Software that bundles an updater shortcut into Startup after archive extraction
  • Security/portable apps extracted with WinRAR that create a startup auto-run by design
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/sfx","setup","install") and InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the dropped file's full path/hash and the parent RAR archive; detonate or read the HTA/VBS content for a download URL and confirm WinRAR version < 7.13 on the host. 2) Contain: delete/quarantine the Startup-folder artifact, isolate the host before next logon (the payload fires at login), and block any URLs/domains found in the script. 3) Hunt: search the org for the same archive SHA256 in mail/download telemetry, for other hosts running unpatched WinRAR, and for follow-on mshta/wscript execution and connections to telegra.ph / gofile.io / S3 storage domains.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where FileName endswith ".hta" or FileName endswith ".vbs" or FileName endswith ".vbe" or FileName endswith ".lnk"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("hta","vbs","vbe","lnk")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 Script Drop into Startup Folder
id: a3f8c1d2-4b6e-4f21-9c7a-1e2d3f4a5b6c
description: Detects WinRAR-family process writing an HTA/VBS/VBE/LNK file into the user Startup folder, consistent with CVE-2025-8088 path-traversal persistence used by Gamaredon in 2025.

logsource:

detection:

#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(winrar|rar|unrar)\.exe$/i
| TargetFileName=/\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\.+\.(hta|vbs|vbe|lnk)$/i

Gamaredon HTA downloader auto-executing from Startup folder at logon (mshta.exe) AIExploitation High
Hunts execution of the persisted Gamaredon HTA downloader: mshta.exe launched at user logon with a command line referencing an .hta inside the Startup folder. Complements the file-write detection by catching execution even when the original drop was missed. Rationale: Pins to the article's specific persistence-to-execution chain (HTA downloader placed in Startup executes at next login) and the LOLBin mshta with a Startup-path command line, a combination with near-zero legitimate occurrence; corroborated by Google/Mandiant noting HTA-in-Startup as the second-stage downloader. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/exploiting-critical-winrar-vulnerability
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1547.001 T1059.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legacy in-house HTA-based dashboard intentionally placed in Startup by IT
  • Vendor application that uses an HTA splash/launcher auto-started at logon
  • Admin troubleshooting that temporarily drops an HTA in Startup
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the mshta command line and the referenced .hta path; read the HTA body for embedded URLs/next-stage (PteroSand VBScript) and check whether a RAR/CVE-2025-8088 drop preceded it. 2) Contain: kill the mshta process, remove the Startup artifact, isolate the host, and block extracted C2/dead-drop domains. 3) Hunt: pivot on the user/host for child wscript/cscript execution, temporary .vbs written-then-deleted (PteroDum), and egress to telegra.ph, gofile.io, or S3 storage providers.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".hta"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "mshta.exe"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has ".hta"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gamaredon stealer exfiltration to S3-compatible cloud storage (Wasabi/Tebi/Intercolo) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts PteroVDoor/PteroPSDoor's 2025 primary exfiltration channel: scripted upload of stolen files to S3-compatible storage at wasabisys.com, tebi.io, or i3storage.com (Intercolo de-fra.i3storage.com) initiated by a script host rather than a browser. High-fidelity because exfil from wscript/powershell/mshta to these specific providers is anomalous. Rationale: Uses the corroborated exfil endpoints (Wasabi=wasabisys.com, Tebi=tebi.io, Intercolo=de-fra.i3storage.com) named as Gamaredon's 2025 primary exfil channel, scoped to script-host initiators to suppress normal browser/backup S3 traffic; ESET's own write-up and the search-confirmed config-rotation (Wasabi→Tebi→Intercolo) second-source the domains. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/gamaredon-2025-leveraging-tunnels-workers-dead-drops-new-alliances/ • https://www.govinfosecurity.com/russias-gamaredon-adapts-tactics-to-target-ukraine-a-32068
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1059.001 T1059.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Corporate backup/sync software legitimately using Wasabi S3 (but normally via its own binary, not wscript/powershell)
  • Developer/DevOps PowerShell scripts pushing artifacts to a sanctioned Wasabi/Tebi bucket
  • A red-team or admin ad-hoc PowerShell aws/s3 upload
  • Telemetry where a browser helper is misattributed as the initiating process
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("aws s3","Backup","veeam") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("backupsvc","svc-backup"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating script host, its command line, and the volume/bytes uploaded; confirm the bucket/host is not a sanctioned corporate storage account. 2) Contain: block the storage FQDNs at the proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and preserve the stealer binary/script for analysis. 3) Hunt: trace back to the persistence/execution chain (mshta-from-Startup, WinRAR drop), enumerate which files were staged/read prior to upload, and sweep other hosts for DNS to the same three providers.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("wasabisys.com","tebi.io","i3storage.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","cmd.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("wasabisys.com","tebi.io","i3storage.com")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gamaredon dead-drop C&C resolution via Telegra.ph and GoFile from script hosts AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts PteroOdd (Telegra.ph API) and PteroEffigy (GoFile) fetching next-stage payloads / resolving C&C from legitimate dead-drop services, requested by a Windows script host. Article-specific because it targets the exact two services named for these downloaders rather than generic LOLBin egress. Rationale: Targets the two specific dead-drop services the article ties to named downloaders (PteroOdd→Telegra.ph API, PteroEffigy→GoFile) and scopes to script-host initiators so normal browser visits to telegra.ph/gofile are excluded; flagged Medium because only the original ESET piece names these two services for these tools. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/gamaredon-2025-leveraging-tunnels-workers-dead-drops-new-alliances/
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user legitimately downloading a shared file from gofile.io that an EDR attributes to a script wrapper
  • Automation/scripts that scrape telegra.ph articles for benign content
  • Browser child processes mis-tagged as the initiating process
  • Security tooling sandboxing a URL that resolves these domains
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the script-host command line and the full URL/telegra.ph path or gofile content ID; pull what was downloaded and decode any retrieved next-stage C&C address. 2) Contain: block telegra.ph/gofile.io egress from the host, isolate it, and add the resolved real C&C to blocklists. 3) Hunt: correlate with preceding HTA/mshta execution and following uploads to wasabisys.com/tebi.io/i3storage.com on the same host, and sweep the org for other script hosts touching these dead-drop services.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("telegra.ph","gofile.io")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","cmd.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("telegra.ph","gofile.io")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port

| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"

      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)

| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

logsource:

detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Zero-Day CVE-2026-20245 Exploited to Gain Root Access

The Hacker News
2026-06-25 8 use cases 2 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

An unknown threat actor exploited a recently disclosed high-severity security flaw impacting Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN as a zero-day at least two months before it was publicly disclosed, according to new findings from Google-owned Mandiant. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-20245 (CVSS score: 7.8), allows an authenticated, local attacker to execute arbitrary commands with elevated privileges

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Rogue SD-WAN control-plane peering from previously-unseen system-IP (auth-bypass / stolen cert)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Cisco SD-WAN Manager privilege escalation via malicious evil_tenant.csv upload (CVE-2026-20245) · [LLM] su elevation from admin into rogue 'troot' account on Cisco SD-WAN appliance
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Rogue 'troot' root account written to /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow on Cisco SD-WAN Manager · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Zero-Day CVE-2026-20245 Exploited to Gain Root Access
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Anti-forensic admin password change-and-revert on Cisco SD-WAN Manager · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Cisco SD-WAN Manager privilege escalation via malicious evil_tenant.csv upload (CVE-2026-20245) AIExploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2026-20245 exploit primitive: upload/processing of a crafted tenant CSV named evil_tenant.csv on a Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager/Controller/Validator that escalates a netadmin account to root. The filename is a confirmed Mandiant IOC and is deleted post-exploit, so the file-create/import event is the catch window. Rationale: evil_tenant.csv is a unique Mandiant-confirmed exploit-file IOC for CVE-2026-20245 with no benign use; a file-import event bearing that exact name on an SD-WAN appliance is near-zero FP. Cross-checked against Google Cloud/Mandiant blog and Cisco PSIRT advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/zero-day-exploitation-cisco-catalyst-sd-wan-manager • https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-sdwan-privesc-4uxFrdzx • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/mandiant-reveals-how-cisco-sd-wan-zero-day-attacks-gained-root-access/
ATT&CKT1068
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate tenant onboarding CSV coincidentally named evil_tenant.csv (extremely unlikely in production)
  • A red-team/pentest engagement replaying the public CVE-2026-20245 PoC
  • Forensic IR staging where an analyst copies the recovered exploit sample back onto a lab appliance
  • Backup/restore of a previously compromised config that still references the filename
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source host is an SD-WAN Manager/Controller/Validator and pull surrounding syslog for the netadmin account that performed the tenant import; check appliance software version against fixed releases (20.9.9.2/20.12.7.2/20.15.4.5/20.15.5.3/20.18.3.1/26.1.1.2). 2) Contain: isolate the appliance from the control plane, force-rotate all admin/netadmin credentials and revoke device certificates, and preserve /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow and config archives before the actor's cleanup script runs. 3) Hunt: search same host for a 'troot' account, su sessions into it, and admin password change-then-revert; check whether a config change was pushed to edge devices.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "evil_tenant.csv"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, Facility, ProcessName, SeverityLevel, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Rogue 'troot' root account written to /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow on Cisco SD-WAN Manager AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence step of the CVE-2026-20245 intrusion: creation of a hidden account named 'troot' with UID 0 / root shell in /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow on a Cisco SD-WAN appliance. The username is a confirmed Mandiant IOC and appliances have no native local-account workflow, so any 'troot' creation is high fidelity. Rationale: 'troot' is a Mandiant/GTIG-confirmed rogue UID-0 account name written to /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow; SD-WAN appliances expose no legitimate Linux useradd workflow, so a 'troot' creation token-matched with passwd/shadow context is high-fidelity persistence. Confirmed via Google Cloud blog and BleepingComputer. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/zero-day-exploitation-cisco-catalyst-sd-wan-manager • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/mandiant-reveals-how-cisco-sd-wan-zero-day-attacks-gained-root-access/
ATT&CKT1136.001
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sysadmin manually creating a local troubleshooting account that happens to contain the string 'troot'
  • Vendor TAC support session creating a temporary diagnostic account
  • Configuration management tooling provisioning local accounts during appliance rebuild
  • Lab/PoC reproduction of the Mandiant intrusion
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the current /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow, confirm a 'troot' entry exists with UID 0 or a login shell, and identify which admin/netadmin session created it and from what source IP. 2) Contain: disable and delete the troot account, kill any active troot sessions, rotate all appliance credentials and revoke device certs, and snapshot disk before the actor's validation/cleanup script removes the entry. 3) Hunt: pivot to su sessions into troot, the evil_tenant.csv import that preceded it, and admin-password change-and-revert anti-forensics; check sibling appliances in the fabric for the same account.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "troot"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("useradd", "/etc/passwd", "/etc/shadow", "new user", "new group", "add-shell")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, Facility, SeverityLevel, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

su elevation from admin into rogue 'troot' account on Cisco SD-WAN appliance AIExploitation High
Hunts the corroborated step where the actor, after creating 'troot', authenticated into it via su from the admin context to obtain a full root shell. PAM/auth syslog records 'session opened for user troot', which is independent telemetry from the file-write detection and fires even if file events aren't captured. Rationale: Mandiant confirmed the admin account used su to access the newly created troot account; PAM 'session opened for user troot' is a unique, deterministic string tied to the named rogue account, making it a clean alert distinct from the file-write detection. Verified against Google Cloud/Mandiant reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/zero-day-exploitation-cisco-catalyst-sd-wan-manager • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/mandiant-reveals-how-cisco-sd-wan-zero-day-attacks-gained-root-access/
ATT&CKT1078.003
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate operator who manually created an account literally named troot then su'd into it
  • Lab/PoC reproduction of the intrusion
  • Backup restoration replaying historical auth logs containing the entry
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the originating account (expected: admin) and source IP of the su, and correlate the session timestamp with the troot account creation and the evil_tenant.csv import. 2) Contain: terminate the troot session, delete the account, isolate the appliance from the SD-WAN control plane, and rotate/revoke admin credentials and certificates. 3) Hunt: review all commands executed in the troot root shell (config exfil, edge-device config push), check for the actor's cleanup/validation script, and sweep peer appliances for matching su-to-troot events.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ProcessName has "su" or SyslogMessage has "su"

Anti-forensic admin password change-and-revert on Cisco SD-WAN Manager AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the operational-security technique Mandiant attributed to this actor: the default/admin password was changed (to enable exfiltration of the SD-WAN fabric config) and then restored to its original value so a logging-in administrator would notice nothing. Surfaces hosts where the admin account password is modified two or more times in a short window. Rationale: Mandiant/GTIG explicitly described the actor changing the admin password to exfiltrate the fabric config then reverting it; two password modifications to the admin account on one appliance inside a short window is the temporal signature of that round-trip. A single change is routine, so the >=2-in-window threshold is the discriminator. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/zero-day-exploitation-cisco-catalyst-sd-wan-manager • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/mandiant-reveals-how-cisco-sd-wan-zero-day-attacks-gained-root-access/
ATT&CKT1098 T1070
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sysadmin who fat-fingers a password reset and immediately corrects it
  • Scheduled credential-rotation tooling that updates then reconciles the admin secret
  • Break-glass procedure that sets and then resets the admin password
  • Vendor TAC session temporarily changing then restoring admin credentials
Suppression filter
// scope to the SD-WAN appliances and drop known rotation tooling identities once enumerated, e.g.:
// | where SyslogMessage !has "cron" and SyslogMessage !has "ansible"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the two+ admin password-change events, confirm whether the final value matches the original (revert), and identify the source IP/session performing them. 2) Contain: force an out-of-band admin password reset and certificate revocation, and review for a fabric-config export occurring between the two changes. 3) Hunt: correlate with troot account creation, su-to-troot sessions, evil_tenant.csv import, and any cleanup/validation script execution; verify no config was pushed to edge devices during the window.
let window = 2h;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("password changed", "password updated", "passwd")
| where SyslogMessage has "admin"
| summarize pwChanges = count(), firstChange = min(TimeGenerated), lastChange = max(TimeGenerated), Samples = make_list(SyslogMessage, 5) by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, window)
| where pwChanges >= 2   // change + revert within the same 2h bucket = anti-forensic round-trip
| sort by lastChange desc
source:linux.syslog admin ("password changed" OR "password updated" OR passwd)
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Change.All_Changes where All_Changes.object_category=user All_Changes.action=modified All_Changes.object="admin" by All_Changes.dest All_Changes.user _time span=2h
| `drop_dm_object_name("All_Changes")`
| stats sum(count) as pwChanges values(user) as actors min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by dest
| where pwChanges >= 2
| `ctime(firstTime)` | `ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Change.All_Changes where All_Changes.object_category=user All_Changes.action=modified All_Changes.object="admin" by All_Changes.dest All_Changes.user _time span=2h
| `drop_dm_object_name("All_Changes")`
| stats sum(count) as pwChanges values(user) as actors min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by dest
| where pwChanges >= 2
| `ctime(firstTime)` | `ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
Rogue SD-WAN control-plane peering from previously-unseen system-IP (auth-bypass / stolen cert) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the initial-access wave Mandiant tied to CVE-2026-20127/CVE-2026-20182 auth-bypass and stolen device certificates: unauthorized control connections (rogue peering) into the SD-WAN fabric from a controller/edge system-IP never observed in the 30-day baseline. Anti-baseline on the peer system-IP parsed from control-connection syslog. Rationale: Mandiant attributed the first/second intrusion waves to rogue peering connections via CVE-2026-20127/20182 auth-bypass or stolen certificates; a control connection from a system-IP absent from the 30-day fabric baseline is the article-specific signature of an unauthorized peer joining the control plane. Lower confidence as it relies on baseline maturity rather than a fixed IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/zero-day-exploitation-cisco-catalyst-sd-wan-manager • https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-sdwan-privesc-4uxFrdzx
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate onboarding of a new vEdge/cEdge or controller into the fabric
  • Datacenter migration or controller IP re-addressing
  • DR failover bringing a standby controller online with a new system-IP
  • Lab/staging device briefly joining the production overlay
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the new peer system-IP against the authorized device inventory and certificate serials; if unknown, treat as rogue. 2) Contain: quarantine/deny the peer at the controller, revoke any suspected stolen device certificate, and verify control-plane policy hasn't been altered. 3) Hunt: on devices the rogue peer touched, look for CVE-2026-20245 follow-on (evil_tenant.csv, troot account, su-to-troot, password change-and-revert) and review whether any config was pushed to edge devices.
let lookback = 30d;
let baseline = Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(lookback) .. ago(1d))
    | where SyslogMessage has "control connection"
    | extend PeerIP = extract(@"system-ip\s+(\d{1,3}(?:\.\d{1,3}){3})", 1, SyslogMessage)
    | where isnotempty(PeerIP)
    | distinct PeerIP;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SyslogMessage has "control connection"
| extend PeerIP = extract(@"system-ip\s+(\d{1,3}(?:\.\d{1,3}){3})", 1, SyslogMessage)
| where isnotempty(PeerIP)
| join kind=leftanti baseline on PeerIP
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, PeerIP, SeverityLevel, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog "control connection" (up OR established OR new)
APPLICATION
index=* (sourcetype="cisco:sdwan" OR sourcetype="cisco:vmanage" OR sourcetype="cisco:vsmart" OR sourcetype="cisco:vbond") "control connection"
| rex field=_raw "system-ip\s+(?<peer_system_ip>\d{1,3}(?:\.\d{1,3}){3})"
| where isnotnull(peer_system_ip)
| stats earliest(_time) as firstTime latest(_time) as lastTime count by host peer_system_ip
| eval ageDays=round((now()-firstTime)/86400,1)
| where ageDays < 1
| `ctime(firstTime)` | `ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - firstTime

simonecorsi/mawesome GitHub Action has been compromised

StepSecurity
2026-06-25 4 use cases 1 technique 3 kill-chain phases detected

On June 24, 2026, an attacker compromised the simonecorsi/mawesome GitHub repository. They force-pushed malicious commits and repointed several version tags to that commit. As a result, any workflow running against those tags after that time executed the attacker's code inside its GitHub Actions runner.

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Compromised simonecorsi/mawesome GitHub Action payload by known hash · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Runner.Worker process memory scrape via /proc on self-hosted GitHub Actions runner · [LLM] First-seen external egress from GitHub Actions Runner.Worker child process
Compromised simonecorsi/mawesome GitHub Action payload by known hash AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the specific malicious payload pushed to simonecorsi/mawesome during the June 24 2026 tag-poisoning compromise, matched by SHA256/SHA1 on self-hosted GitHub Actions runners monitored by EDR. Fires on file write or process execution of the imposter-commit artifact inside the runner. Rationale: Pivots on the article's three pre-extracted IOCs (SHA256 9f93d77d... and the two SHA1s) which are the imposter-commit payload; a hash match is near-zero-FP, so this is a clean alerting rule for any self-hosted runner that executed a poisoned mawesome tag. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/github-action-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066 • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/detecting-and-mitigating-the-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2025/03/18/supply-chain-compromise-third-party-tj-actionschanged-files-cve-2025-30066-and-reviewdogaction
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sandboxed runner for analysis
  • EDR/AV quarantine copy of the file re-scanned generating a benign file event
  • Threat-intel team staging the IOC file on a host for YARA testing
  • Backup/forensic image mounting that re-reads the captured payload
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") or FolderPath has_any ("\\Quarantine\\", "/quarantine/"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the host is a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner and pull the workflow run that executed it; identify which mawesome tag/SHA was referenced and the repo. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the runner, rotate ALL secrets exposed to that workflow (GITHUB_TOKEN, cloud OIDC roles, registry creds, signing keys) and pin the action to a trusted commit SHA or remove it. 3) HUNT: Search other runners for the same hashes, review egress from the runner during the run window, and check downstream artifacts/packages built by that pipeline for tampering.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in (badSHA256) or SHA1 in (badSHA1) or InitiatingProcessSHA256 in (badSHA256) or InitiatingProcessSHA1 in (badSHA1)

Runner.Worker process memory scrape via /proc on self-hosted GitHub Actions runner AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the core mawesome/tj-actions-style payload behaviour: a child process spawned by the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker reading /proc/<pid>/maps or /proc/<pid>/mem to scrape CI/CD secrets from runner memory. Article-specific because it pivots on Runner.Worker as the parent plus the in-image label 'Runner.Worker Memory Scrape'. Rationale: Corroborated by Sysdig/Wiz analyses of the identical tj-actions payload which 'identifies the Runner.Worker process, opens its memory mappings and regex-searches for secrets'; the Runner.Worker parent + /proc maps/mem access is the high-fidelity credential-access signal the thin article only labels as 'Runner.Worker Memory Scrape'. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/detecting-and-mitigating-the-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066 • https://www.wiz.io/blog/github-action-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066
ATT&CKT1003.007 T1552
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Runner self-diagnostic or crash-dump tooling (gcore/dd) reading worker memory during a hang
  • Performance profilers (perf, py-spy) attached to a build process inside CI
  • Custom debugging step in a workflow that intentionally inspects /proc for troubleshooting
  • Container runtime health checks reading /proc/<pid>/status (excluded by maps/mem filter)
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("py-spy","perf record","/proc/self/status","/proc/meminfo") )
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full command line of the child process and the workflow YAML that ran; confirm whether a memory-read step was legitimately authored or injected by a third-party action. 2) CONTAIN: Treat every secret available to that job as compromised — rotate tokens/OIDC roles immediately and isolate the runner from further job dispatch. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same Runner.Worker parent across all runners for /proc memory reads, base64-encoded stdout, and any outbound POST to gist.githubusercontent.com or unknown hosts in the same run window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "Runner.Worker"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/proc/" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("maps","mem")
| where FileName in~ ("python3","python","node","perl","ruby","sh","bash","cat","dd","gcore")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has "Runner.Worker"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "/proc/" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("maps","mem")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python3","python","node","perl","ruby","bash","sh","cat","dd","gcore")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
